---
title: "Leakage, concretely"
description: "A working taxonomy of leakage mechanisms, and which tool addresses each one."
---

"Data leakage" gets used for several unrelated failures. Separating them is
useful, because they have different symptoms and different fixes — and because
a tool that handles one of them is not thereby handling the others.

## The mechanisms

### Preprocessing leakage

A transformation is estimated on data that includes the test fold, then applied
to both sides. Global median imputation, z-scoring against the full matrix,
variance filtering before splitting, and — worst of the family — univariate
feature selection against the outcome across all samples.

*Symptom:* performance degrades sharply when the pipeline is rerun with
preprocessing moved inside the resampling loop. With aggressive feature
selection on wide data, the drop can be most of the apparent signal.

*Addressed by:* `bioLeak::fit_resample()` and `bioLeak::impute_guarded()`
re-estimate preprocessing inside each training fold; `fastml()` keeps
preprocessing inside the resampling path for the workflows it fits.

### Dependence leakage

Samples in the training set are not independent of samples in the test set.
Repeated measures on the same subject, technical replicates, samples from the
same batch or sequencing run, patients from the same site, or near-duplicate
rows.

*Symptom:* held-out performance is good, but performance on a genuinely new
subject, batch or site collapses. This is the mechanism that most often survives
peer review.

*Addressed by:* `splitGraph` makes the dependency structure explicit and derives
what it implies for splitting; `bioLeak::make_split_plan()` builds folds that
respect it; `bioLeak::check_split_overlap()` verifies they did.

### Temporal leakage

The model trains on data recorded after what it is asked to predict. Common
whenever samples carry a collection date and the split ignores it, and in
clinical data where a measurement is only ordered once a diagnosis is suspected.

*Symptom:* excellent retrospective performance, no prospective performance.

*Addressed by:* `splitGraph` models `Timepoint` nodes and precedence edges;
`bioLeak::make_split_plan(mode = "time_series")` supports `horizon`, `purge` and
`embargo` gaps.

### Target leakage

A predictor is a proxy for, or a consequence of, the outcome. A treatment code
that only exists post-diagnosis, an identifier correlated with case status, a
derived feature computed from the label.

*Symptom:* implausibly high performance, usually attributable to one or two
features.

*Addressed by:* `bioLeak::audit_leakage()` runs univariate and multivariate
target-leakage scans. Excluding identifier columns (`fastml(exclude = )`) is the
cheap first defence.

### Group-structure confounding

Not leakage between folds, but between variables: the outcome is associated with
a batch or site, so a model that learns batch learns the outcome. The split can
be perfectly clean and the result still meaningless.

*Symptom:* a batch-association test is significant; performance is explained as
well by batch as by biology.

*Addressed by:* `bioLeak::audit_leakage()` runs batch and fold association
tests; `bioLeak::confounder_sensitivity()` quantifies how much the estimate
moves when a confounder is controlled.

## Coverage map

| Mechanism | splitGraph | bioLeak | fastml |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Preprocessing leakage | | ● | ● |
| Dependence leakage | ● | ● | ○ |
| Temporal leakage | ● | ● | ○ |
| Target leakage | | ● | ○ |
| Group-structure confounding | ○ | ● | |

: ● directly addressed  ○ partially, or only when configured {tbl-colwidths="[40,20,20,20]"}

The blank cells are the honest part. `fastml` will not tell you that your
`patient_id` column is a proxy for the outcome, and `splitGraph` will not notice
that you z-scored the matrix before you built the graph.

## Glossary

The three packages use these terms consistently. Where a term has a wider
meaning in the literature, the sense used here is the narrower one.

**Block** — a coarser grouping than the splitting unit, which ideally should not
straddle a fold. In a `split_spec`, `block_vars`.

**Embargo** — in time-ordered evaluation, a gap after the test window during
which training samples are also excluded.

**Guarded** — a workflow in which preprocessing and fitting are re-estimated
within each resampling split, rather than once over the whole dataset.

**Group / splitting unit** — the entity that must stay on one side of a split.
Usually a subject; sometimes a study or a site. In a `split_spec`, `group_var`.

**LSI (leakage severity index)** — bioLeak's summary of how much apparent
performance is attributable to a leakage mechanism. `delta_lsi()` compares two
evaluations on the same data.

**Permutation gap** — the difference between observed performance and
performance under label permutation within the same resampling scheme. A gap
near zero means the scheme is not finding signal; a large gap under a *broken*
scheme is evidence of leakage rather than of skill.

**Purge** — in time-ordered evaluation, removal of training samples whose
information window overlaps the test window.

**`split_spec`** — splitGraph's versioned, tool-agnostic description of a split:
which column is the group, which are blocks, which is time, which is the
stratum. Serialisable to JSON against a shipped schema.

**Severed** — of a leakage finding, structurally eliminated by the split mode
chosen, as opposed to merely unmeasured.

## Further reading

The packages implement ideas that are not original to them. The papers listed on
the [Papers](papers.qmd) page cite the primary sources; the standard references
on leakage in applied machine learning are the place to start if the taxonomy
above is new.
